Precise local magnetic field measurements are crucial for characterizing novel magnetic materials, detecting early-stage cancers via biomagnetic signatures, and probing fundamental physics via neutrino or dark matter interactions. Although techniques like SQUIDs, Hall probes, atomic magnetometers, and Ac-circuits can detect magnetic fields globally or over large areas, resolving sharp local variations remains difficult. This paper presents a new approach utilizing atomic interferometry to measure local field changes with exceptional sensitivity by observing the Meffner effect in superconductors. Experimental results demonstrate that the method detects local fields as weak as approximately 0.14 G (or 1.4 × 10−5 T) with an average sensitivity of roughly 0.7 G (7 × 10−2 T) per square root of Hertz at zero frequency. These sensitivities were achieved without requiring extremely high resolution in the atomic sensor itself; instead, the approach relies on integrating long, highly sensitive atomic clocks to build up precision over time.

We examine the phenomenology of the minimal scoto-seesaw model, the simplest extension of the basic Standard Model capable of neutrino mass generation via the seesaw mechanism and simultaneously accounting for WIMP dark matter through the portal interaction. Although this minimal configuration with two additional right-handed neutrinos and a singlet scalar fails to fit all neutrino oscillation data, we demonstrate that it remains viable as an effective low-energy framework. Furthermore, assuming it operates as such, we explore potential high-energy extensions. Our analysis reveals that while various minimal ultraviolet completions can ensure vacuum stability up to approximately $10^{14}$ GeV and satisfy dark matter relic abundance requirements through annihilations into neutrinos, achieving both vacuum stability beyond $10^{14}$ geV and correct dark matter relic density simultaneously demands U.V completions involving additional scalar fields, possibly light ones. Additionally, we investigate dark matter production mechanisms beyond thermal freeze-out, including freeze-in and thermal initial overproduction, and find that dark matter can satisfy observed abundance levels across all these scenarios with feasible collider signatures.
